catalog_quote: 2.6 Stress. Stress is predictable when morphophonemic rules are applied. In a verb-final clause, enclitics and one classification of suffixes are unstressed and are usually composed of a short /‚/ [= schwa-type vowel] followed by one consonant, or just short /‚/. The primary clause stress then falls on the syllable immediately preceding these suffixes or clitics, which is usually CVC(C).48 The stress pattern of a typical clause is seen in figure 2.13 ... Stress levels are based on the pitch pattern and amplitude as shown by the Speech Analyzer tool and impressionistic perception. ... In noun phrases, clitics and one classification of noun suffixes are unstressed and the noun word receives the phrase stress, which is usually a secondary stress in a verbal clause. A prefix is likely to receive tertiary stress in the clause, or secondary stress under some conditions, rather than being unst…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim in the held Dieterman 2008 text at sec. 2.6 pp. 31-32 with fn. 48. (2) The deciding source is a 2008 phonology monograph (revised 2002 dissertation) with instrumental backing, by the language's principal modern describer; Glottolog has nothing better (4 refs, one phonology = this). (3) Two further primary statements were fetched sources now from open SIL/UND copies and both support the 'morphological' coding: Nordell's 1977 rule assigns stress to the root-final vowel with the Root bracket in the structural description, and Dieterman & McCarty 2018 describe default word-final prominence minus a closed list of short-ë suffixes that are never stressed — the same generalisation as Dieterman 2008 (stress on the syllable preceding the unstressed suffix/enclitic class, i.e. root/stem-final). sources.quote: 'las palabras que tienen más de una sílaba se pronuncian con un tono de voz más alto y fuerte al final de estas, es decir, llevan un acento prosódico en la última sílaba. Como el acento prosódico es predecible, no es necesario escribir el acento ortográfico … Sin embargo, existe una lista relativamente corta de sufijos que, al presentarse al final de una palabra, nunca van acentuados. Todos los sufijos de esta lista contienen ë, una vocal sencilla' (listed: -ë, -ëch, -ëk, -ëts, -ëm, -ën, -ëp, -ët, -ëxë, -në, -pë, -xë); complex ë nuclei (ëë, ëꞌ …) are stressed when final; place names in -ëm nev

sources.citation: Nordell, Norman. 1977 (Jan.). Morphophonemics of Guichicovi Mixe verb roots. Unpublished ms., 14 pp. SIL Mexico Branch, Bartholomew Collection of Unpublished Materials (SIL Language & Culture Archives 43911).
sources.quote: Rule 1 Stress Placement: [+syl] -> [+stress] / [ ___ (V) C1 ]_Root [-seg], i.e. the last vowel of the root is stressed; ex. (1) #tuk]R# -> [túhk] 'he picked it', (2) #wɨtít]R % wɨp# -> [wɨdíTɨp] 'he should stroll' (root-final syllable stressed, suffix -ɨp unstressed).

sources.note: Dieterman 2008:24 reports Wichmann positing a seventh, reduced vowel (schwa) 'that is never stressed' for this variety; his per-language phonology summaries may state the stress rule independently of Dieterman/Nordell and bear on whether the unstressed-suffix class is phonologically (reduced vowel) rather than morphologically defined.
